title: Stata Companion Guide
text:
Preface
This is a guide to learning Stata. The structure roughly follows the 2nd edition of Statistics Minus the Math: https://minusthemath.com/2e/
Even if you are not using that textbook, you are welcome to use this guide.
Some similar materials are available for learning R at the sister site: https://favero-nate.github.io/companion-guides/r/
If you wish to download a PDF of the text from this guide, one is available here: https://favero-nate.github.io/companion-guides/stata/Stata-Companion-Guide.pdf

title: Stata Companion Guide
text:
Contents
The main contents of this site will consist of videos you can watch, organized into four parts that can be taught alone or alongside the first several chapters of Statistics Minus the Math. Each part has 3-4 videos.
Below each video, there is a list of key concepts/commands from the video, along with examples of the commands being used.
In the final section of Parts 1-4, I provide an exercise where you can try out what you just learned with a different dataset.

title: Stata Companion Guide
text:
Accessing Stata
To get started using Stata on your own, you will probably need to install Stata on your device (requires buying a license) or install software allowing you to access Stata remotely through your school. Exact instructions will vary, depending on the type of device you have and the manner of access you are using. If you are at a university or other school, please consult their resources on how to access Stata from your device.

title: Introduction
text:
Key concepts/commands:
Dataset source: https://onlinestatbook.com/2/case_studies/binge.html

title: Introduction
text:
use: load in a dataset
use "https://learndata.net/binge.dta"
clear: empty out any dataset so a new one can be loaded in
clear
To make a simple comment in a do-file, use // or *
// This is a note to myself, called a "comment"
* Here is another way to leave a note
To make a multi-line (or partial-line) comment, use /* to start and */ to end
/*
Here is a rather long comment.
Maybe it is a note about how some of
the variables were measured.
*/

title: Simple Graphs
text: Key concepts/commands:

title: Simple Graphs
text:
graph bar: create a simple bar graph
graph bar, over(sex_text)
graph pie: create a simple pie chart
graph pie, over(sex_text)
hist: create a histogram
hist modrunk
kdensity: create a k-density plot
kdensity modrunk
graph box: create a boxplot
graph box modrunk, hor
findit: find a package to install
findit vioplot
vioplot: create a violin plot (requires installation of user package)
vioplot modrunk, hor
stripplot: create a strip plot (requires installation of user package)
stripplot modrunk, jitter(10)

title: Variable Types
text: Key concepts/commands:

title: Variable Types
text:
numeric variables: many different specific numeric types, but they are shown in black or blue in the Data Editor
string variables: these are text (non-numeric) variables, and they are shown in red in the Data Editor
codebook: show variable information, including the numeric values underlying any “value labels” (for variables showing up in blue)
codebook u_fam

title: Put it into Practice
text:
Now it’s time to try things out for yourself. Complete each of the following steps, based on what we learned in this chapter.
Unless your instructor tells you otherwise, use a do-file to execute all commands needed to accomplish the following:

Load in the social media posts dataset (posts.dta). You can download it here and save it on your computer. Or you can load the file directly into Stata through the web at the following URL: https://learndata.net/posts.dta


Select four variables to examine. Make sure to choose at least one qualitative (or ordinal) variable and one quantitative variable. Note that binary variables (with values of only 0 and 1) are considered qualitative variables.
For each of these four variables, make at least two graphs. If you are submitting your work to an instructor, you will probably want to save a copy of each graph in a Word document, which you can then submit to show you completed this assignment.
See the video at the bottom of this page for guidance on getting graphs out of Stata and into a Word doc. You can try using copy-paste, although this may not work if you have a remote access setup for using Stata. Another option is to take a screenshot and then paste this into your Word doc. One final option is to click the “save” icon in the window showing the graph, allowing you to save the graph as its own file in a folder of your choosing; before clicking the “Save” button, you will need to change the setting under “Save as type” to something like a PNG or JPEG that can easily be read into Word. In Word, you can then navigate to “insert” a “picture” from your device.

After completing all of this, you should save your do-file in a folder that is convenient to access. It is a good idea at the end of your work to try clearing out your Stata session (e.g., typing “clear” in the command box and then hitting Enter) and then running your entire do-file at once, to make sure you have a clean do-file that can fully execute. If you are submitting work to an instructor, they will likely want you to send them both your do-file and a Word doc containing your graphs.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text: Key concepts/commands:

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
sum: show descriptive statistics for quantitative variables
sum modrunk u_fam, detail
* and ?: wildcard characters
sum ?_*
tab modrunk: show a frequency table
tab modrunk

title: File Types
text:
Key concepts:
You can download the zip file referenced in this lesson here: https://learndata.net/binge.zip

title: File Types
text:
zip file: a compressed file that can contain several files/folders within it
Excel file: not a plain text file, created for use with Microsoft Excel and uses file ending “.xls” or “.xlsx”
fixed width file: a plain text file format that uses a fixed number of characters for each column (requires access to a dictionary to indicate each column’s width), used to be popular but now less widely used
tab delimited file: a plain text file format that uses tabs to indicate the next column
R file: not a plain text file, created for use with the statistical program R and uses file ending “.Rdata”, “.Rda”, or “.Rds”
Stata data file: not a plain text file, created for use with the statistical program Stata and uses file ending “.dta”
comma delimited file: a plain text file format that uses commas to indicate the next column, can use file ending “.csv”

title: Importing Files
text:
Key concepts/commands:
You can download the zip file referenced in this lesson here: https://learndata.net/binge.zip

title: Importing Files
text:
cd: set the “working directory,” which is the default folder on your computer in which Stata will look for files and output files
cd "C:\Users\favero\OneDrive - american.edu\minus the math\companion guides\datasets\02\example files"
import excel: read in an Excel document as a dataset
import excel using binge.xls, firstrow
help: used to access Stata help files, often for a specific command
help import excel
insheet: old command to read in a plain text file
insheet using binge.tab
import delimited: a newer way to read in a delimited plain text file
import delimited binge.csv

title: Put it into Practice
text:
Now it’s time to try things out for yourself. Complete each of the following steps, based on what we learned in this chapter.
Unless your instructor tells you otherwise, use an do-file to execute all code needed to accomplish the following (note: step 1 can be completed outside of Stata):

Download the ed_nonprofits.zip file, which can be found here and save it on your computer. Extract the files (unzip it) in a convenient folder on your computer.
Set your working director to the folder where the unzipped files are located. Import each file of the three files from the zip file into Stata, one at a time. Create a file where you can record notes (e.g., a Word file). For each file, write down the name of each file (including the file ending), and then indicate which variable appears first (as the first column) in each file.
Generate summary statistics for quantitative variables for the following variables: staff_boardmmbr_2024, finance_rev_indvdon_pct, staff_fulltime_2023, pplsrv_numserved. You can use any of the three files, since all have equivalent data.
Generate frequency tables for the following variables: sizestrata, peer_group.

After completing all of this, you should save your do-file in a folder that is convenient to access. If you are submitting work to an instructor, they will likely want you to send them both your do-file and a Word doc containing your results for items 2, 3, and 4 above.

title: Transforming Variables
text: Key concepts/commands:

title: Transforming Variables
text:
destring: convert a string variable to a numeric variable
destring iep blackhispanic ell thgrmathela, replace ignore("%" "#VALUE!")
rename: rename a variable
rename thgrmathela combined_score
gen: create a new variable
gen z_ell = (ell - 13.79202) / 12.33479
log(): a function to create a log transformation (based on the natural log)
gen log_ell = log(ell)
order: rearrange the ordering of variables
order log_ell, after(ell)
drop: delete variables (or delete observations, as we will learn about later)
drop z_ell
egen: another way to create a new variable, relying on a specific set of functions for creating new variables
egen z_ell = std(ell)

title: Associations (for Quantitative Variables)
text: Key concepts/commands:

title: Associations (for Quantitative Variables)
text:
corr: calculate correlations among variables
corr overallscore combined_score
twoway scatter: create a scatter plot
twoway scatter overallscore combined_score
twoway lfit: create a linear (regression) trendline
twoway (scatter overallscore combined_score) (lfit overallscore combined_score)

title: Regression
text: Key concepts/commands:

title: Regression
text:
reg: run a linear (OLS) regression
reg overallscore combined_score ell iep blackhispanic economicneedindex
monospace fonts: often used to display text in programming contexts, also useful for displaying raw text output from many statistical software packages

title: Qualitative-Quantitative Relationships
text:
Key concepts/commands:
Note: Part 4 of this Guide is longer than prior parts, so you may want to split it into two sessions: this page can serve as session A, and the remaining pages can serve as session B.
There are two videos that go with this page:

title: Qualitative-Quantitative Relationships
text:
clear all: empty out not just the current dataset but also other things stored in Stata’s memory
clear all
bys: repeat a command for different subsets of the data
bys schooltype: sum combined_score, detail
over() option: for many graphs, allows for grouping by a qualitative variable
graph box combined_score, over(schooltype)
encode: create a numeric version of a string variable
encode overallgrade, gen(grade_factor)
replace: change (some) values for a variable
replace grade_A = 1 if overallgrade == "A"
if: impose a restriction on a command (e.g., only apply to certain observations)
replace grade_A = 1 if overallgrade == "A"
==: check whether two things are equal
replace grade_A = 1 if overallgrade == "A"
!=: means “not equal” (the exclamation point means “not”)
replace grade_A = 0 if overallgrade != "A" & overallgrade != ""
missing option with tab: include missing values in frequency table
tab overallgrade grade_A, missing
gen() option with tab: create binary variables indicating each value from a frequency table
tab overallgrade, gen(grade_)
save: save the current dataset
save "nycschools_modified.dta", replace

title: Qualitative-Qualitative Relationships
text: Key concepts/commands:

title: Qualitative-Qualitative Relationships
text:
col and row options with tab: show percentages by column/row in a two-way table
tab schooltype overallgrade, col
title() option: add a title at the top (of a graph)
graph bar, over(overallgrade) over(schooltype) title("Overall school grade by school type")
ylabels() option: choose the y axis labels (for a graph)
graph bar, over(overallgrade) over(schooltype) ylabels(0 10 20 30)
#(#)# where each # is replaced with a specific number: indicate a sequence of numbers, counting up by a fixed amount
graph bar, over(overallgrade) over(schooltype) ylabels(0(10)30)
rows() option with a by() option: choose the number of rows to use
graph bar, over(overallgrade) by(schooltype, rows(1))
stack asyvars percentage options: make a bar chart into a stacked bar chart
graph bar, over(overallgrade) over(schooltype) stack asyvars percentage

title: Regression with Qualitative Variables
text: Key concepts/commands:

title: Regression with Qualitative Variables
text:
log close: stop any log currently being kept
capture log close
log: keep a log file
log using ch4_part3_log.txt, replace text
i. prefix: treat a (numeric) variable as a factor (qualitative) variable
reg combined_score i.schooltype_factor, base

title: Instructor Notes
text:
Sample course outline
I’ve constructed this outline to span 10 weeks, since a typical 15 week course on introductory statistics may reserve some weeks for exams or other content.

title: Instructor Notes
text:
Week 1: Getting Started (Stata Companion Guide Part 1)
Depending on what kind of setup you have for running your software (e.g., in a virtual desktop environment), students may struggle to figure out how to transfer graphs into Word or whatever format you use for student submissions. You may want to walk students through how to do this. You might also want to show students what it means to have a clean script file that will execute in full.


Week 2: Description, File Types (Stata Companion Guide Part 2)
Especially relevant to this chapter, many students struggle with basic file management. You might want to spend some time showing them what it looks like to have a good folder structure for data work (e.g., using the cloud file storage system provided by your school).


Week 3: Transformations, Associations (Stata Companion Guide Part 3)
I designed the “Put it into Practice” assignment with the intention that students would get some practice with executing transformations and regressions in software The actual transformations and regression they perform may not be very useful/informative. Still, this exercise can set the scene for a follow-up discussion in class (e.g., comparing regression results from standardized vs. unstandardized variables).


Week 4: Recoding Variables and Comparing Means/Medians (Stata Companion Guide - first page of Part 4)
Part 4 of the guide has more material (and is more difficult) than the other parts, so I recommend splitting it across two weeks. In this first week, you can cover just the section titled “Qualitative-Quantitative Relationships.”


Week 5: Crosstabs/Graphs and Regression with Qualitative Variables (Stata Companion Guide - rest of Part 4)
If you are using the Statistics Minus the Math textbook, note that this week’s “Put it into Practice” dataset does not currently match Ch. 4 of the textbook, but I plan to update the textbook in the future so that they match.


Week 6: More Data Management
https://stata.jeremiahdittmar.info/data-manipulation/
Note: To align with Ch. 6 of Statistics Minus the Math, I would also show students how to add chi-square test results to a crosstab using the “chi2” option (see help file for tabulate twoway).


Week 7: Subsetting and Labeling Data
https://stats.oarc.ucla.edu/stata/modules/ubsetting-data/
https://stats.oarc.ucla.edu/stata/modules/labeling-data/


Week 8: Making Nice Graphs
https://stata.jeremiahdittmar.info/graphics/


Week 9: Making Nice Tables
https://repec.sowi.unibe.ch/stata/estout/esttab.html


Week 10: Plotting Predicted Values from Regression
https://stats.oarc.ucla.edu/stata/seminars/interactions-stata/
